extracted.intended_audience: Undergraduate students in Math 444/445 (Geometry for Teachers); students learning to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing clear, precise, and readable mathematical proofs (paragraph-style prose, formula usage, and presentation conventions) aimed at undergraduate students learning proof-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof is designed to communicate the truth of a mathematical statement and the correctness of your argument to a human reader; ordinary prose (complete sentences organized into paragraphs) is much better suited than terse symbolic statements or two-column proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although you might initially construct the argument as terse symbolic statements, when you write it up use paragraph-style prose. Paragraph-style proofs are easier to read and comprehend than symbolic ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English
rubrics_metrics.description: All mathematical writing should follow the same conventions of grammar, usage, punctuation, and spelling as any other writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complete sentences, correct punctuation (including a period at the end of every sentence), avoid run-on sentences, attend to subject-verb agreement and parallel structure, and use correct spelling and capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware who your audience is and what they already know; write proofs to convince that audience of the theorem and correctness of your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this course: write as if convincing a fellow student in the class. You may assume the reader knows the same background material, but not the proof of this particular theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the right amount of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much detail to include based on your audience; if an argument seems tedious or unclear to you, work it out fully before deciding to omit parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the omitted details would be obvious to the intended reader, they may be left out; otherwise include just enough so the reader gets the 'Aha!' experience and the grader can see you understood the details. Deciding this balance is subtle and requires judgement and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what you’re proving and label results clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state the theorem (or proposition, lemma, corollary) you are proving and label it accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the result in one or more precise English sentences (e.g., 'Theorem: If x is a real number, then x^2 ≥ 0.'). Use labels (Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Corollary) to signal the role of the result. Formatting notes: in typeset work use bold 'Theorem' and italics for the statement; in handwritten work underline 'Theorem'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show where proofs begin and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proof should begin with the word 'Proof' and end with QED or a suitable end-of-proof symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Proof' at the start; finish with 'QED' (quod erat demonstrandum) or a symbol such as a square to mark the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision (define terms and quantify symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mathematical statement must have a precise mathematical meaning: terms must be well-defined and symbols must be previously defined or appropriately quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What does it mean?' for every claim. If you write f(a) > 0, specify whether this is for all a ∈ R, there exists a, or a particular a introduced earlier. Ensure every term/symbol has a clear definition or quantification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify every claim (why is it true?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mathematical conclusion must be justified by one of the accepted means of mathematical justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable justifications: by an axiom; by a previously proved theorem; by a definition; by hypothesis; by a previous step in the current proof; or by the rules of logic. Explicitly indicate which is being used where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly (explain ideas and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond precision, ensure writing is comprehensible: include intuitive explanations and an outline for longer arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arguments longer than a few sentences, begin by describing informally what you'll do and why, then carry out the proof, then summarize what you've done. If using a non-direct method, state the type (e.g., 'We will prove the contrapositive' or 'We will prove by contradiction'). Intermix words and formulas to indicate why steps follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal vs. informal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear which parts of the exposition are formal logical steps and which are informal intuition or motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal parts to motivate or sketch ideas, and formal parts to give precise definitions and logical steps; ensure the reader can easily tell the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person singular sparingly; prefer 'we'
rubrics_metrics.description: Most mathematical writing avoids 'I' and uses 'we' to refer to the writer and reader when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' whenever it can reasonably be interpreted as 'writer and reader' (e.g., 'We will prove the theorem by induction on n.'). Use 'I' only when genuinely referring to yourself (e.g., 'I learned this technique from...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid most abbreviations in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Common shorthand abbreviations used on the board or in notes should generally not be used in written exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 's.t.' (such that), 'w.r.t.' (with respect to), 'w.l.o.g.' (without loss of generality), and 'iff'. Acceptable abbreviations are those standard in formal writing such as 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' — but use them correctly. Opinion: 'iff' can hinder understanding and should generally be avoided in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread your proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your proofs from beginning to end after finishing to catch mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful proofreading will reveal many silly or subtle errors; don't skip this step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and formulas judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas are indispensable for clarity but must be used judiciously: excessive symbolic use can make writing obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbolic formulas when they make a sentence clearer (e.g., 'Let f be defined by f(x)=x^2+x'), but balance with prose to keep exposition readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose inline vs. displayed formulas appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Single symbols and short, simple formulas belong inline; large or especially important formulas should be displayed (centered on their own line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display complex expressions (summations, integrals, matrices, big fractions) or any formula that is important/large; small/simple symbols and expressions should appear naturally in running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give every symbol/formula a grammatical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mathematical symbol or formula, whether inline or displayed, must serve a definite grammatical function as part of a sentence; formulas cannot stand alone as entire sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical grammatical functions: (1) an expression representing a mathematical object used as a noun, or (2) a complete symbolic mathematical statement used as a clause. Read sentences aloud to test grammatical function. Example: 'If x > 2, we see that x^2 + x must be greater than 6.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed formulas correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: If a displayed formula ends a sentence, it must be followed by a period; likewise other punctuation (comma, semicolon) that would be required if the formula were inline must appear after a displayed equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is easy to forget — ensure displayed equations carry the same sentence punctuation as their inline equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation/operator symbols only to connect mathematical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols representing relations (e.g., =, >, ∈, ⊆) or operators (e.g., +, −, ∩) should connect mathematical symbols, not words with symbols or words with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BAD example: 'If x is a real number that is > 2, then x^2 + x must be > 6.' GOOD alternatives: 'If x is a real number such that x > 2, then we must have x^2 + x > 6.' or 'If x is a real number that is greater than 2, then x^2 + x must be greater than 6.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Format built-up expressions to fit or display them
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex expressions (summations, integrals, matrices, large fractions) should be displayed or written so they fit naturally on a line without awkward spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a slash for inline fractions like 'x/(y+2)'. If a fraction is large or complicated and needs a horizontal bar, display it. Small numerical fractions such as 1/2 can be included inline if sized appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning sentences with mathematical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a sentence with a symbol makes it hard for the reader to recognize the sentence start (you can't capitalize a symbol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reword to begin with words, e.g., instead of 'f is a continuous function' write 'The function f is continuous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing two formulas separated only by punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two formulas separated only by a comma or punctuation look like one long formula and can be confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpose words to separate formulas. BAD example: 'If x ≠ 0, x^2 > 0.' Better: 'If x ≠ 0, then x^2 > 0.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not replace English logical words with their symbol counterparts in sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical-symbols like ∃, ∀, ∧, ∨, ¬, ⇒, ⇔ should not replace the corresponding words in English sentences except as part of complete symbolic logic formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless writing in formal logic, write out 'for every', 'there exists', 'and', 'or', 'not', 'implies', 'if and only if' in words. Possible exceptions: ⇒ and ⇔ are sometimes used to connect formulas or letters representing statements, but must not be used to connect English statements. Examples: 'We will prove that (a) ⇔ (b) by first showing (a) ⇒ (b) and then (b) ⇒ (a).' is acceptable; 'The fact that x is nonzero ⇒ x^2 is positive.' is BAD.
